% TODO(title): the paper now presents FeRRy; the old title named HERMES.
\title{FeRRy: RF-Aware Mission Planning for Federated Learning with Drones as Data Mules}
% Authors: omitted for double-anonymous review. The \author block (names,
% affiliations, emails) is kept in the Overleaf copy, not in this public repo;
% restore it there for the camera-ready.

\maketitle

% Abstract: the short hybrid of abstract_revision.md, adopted 8 Oct 2026
% (the document keeps the earlier versions and the audit of the original).
\begin{abstract}
Federated learning (FL) supports privacy by letting devices train a shared model
without sharing their raw data, but assumes every device can reach a central
server. In contested and disaster-zone deployments that assumption fails:
devices that are out of range or poorly connected are skipped repeatedly, and
federation rounds stall. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) acting as data mules can
carry model updates to and from such devices, but a mule has a finite mission
budget, and its radio decides how far it reaches. We present FeRRy, a
Federated RF-aware Routing framework that treats a mule's reach as a decision,
through three components. First, before each flight, a band-aware mission planner
chooses the contact band class, which trades range for rate, together with the
route, under one feasibility test of per-device deadlines and the mission budget,
with a coverage term that keeps devices from being starved. Second, in flight,
the mule re-plans the rest of its route when the observed channel uses up the
plan's slack, and a per-stop rule can switch to a faster band and reorder the
remaining stops, each reorder checked by the same test. Third, a hierarchical
aggregation layer merges updates on each mule, then across mules at the edge
server, weighting stale updates down. In a prototype whose server, mules and
devices run as separate processes over TCP and train a real intrusion-detection
model on CICIoT2023, with flight time, the radio channel and energy simulated, we
compare FeRRy with seven baseline schedulers, including adaptations of
mobile-transporter federated learning (FedEx), Oort, FedCS and a Whittle-index
age-of-update scheduler. With six devices, one mule and a moderate budget, FeRRy
reaches the target accuracy 27--31\% sooner than each baseline, because its plan
chooses a long-reach narrow band that removes most of the transit between stops.
Under tight budgets, it keeps the age of updates about a quarter lower than
age-of-information schedulers and, with 24 devices, reaches the target 12\%
sooner than FedEx's route. Its plans stay within a tight budget in 70\% of
missions, overrunning by only 8.5\,s on average otherwise.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Decentralized learning, federated learning, UAV data mules, tactical edge computing, mobile relay networks
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Disaster response, wildfire monitoring, agricultural sensing, and tactical
field operations increasingly depend on edge devices deployed where fixed
network infrastructure is sparse, damaged, or unavailable. These devices
capture observations that may be difficult or impossible to reproduce, such as
sensor measurements from an isolated field site, imagery from damaged
infrastructure, or telemetry from vehicles operating beyond cellular
coverage~\cite{zeng2016wireless, song2022comprehensive}. Yet these are also the
environments most likely to experience denied, disrupted, intermittent, and
limited (DDIL) connectivity, where towers may lose power, backhaul may become
congested, and terrain or distance may prevent persistent communication with a
central server~\cite{gupta2015survey}.

Federated learning (FL) is well suited to this setting because devices train on
their local observations and exchange model updates instead of transferring raw
datasets~\cite{mcmahan2017communication, kostage2025hifins}. However, reducing
the amount of data transferred does not remove the need for connectivity. In a
DDIL deployment, the practical bottleneck becomes \emph{reachability}: if a
device cannot contact the federation server, its update cannot contribute to
the global model. As connectivity deteriorates, rounds increasingly close with
only a subset of participants, time out while waiting for unavailable clients,
or fail to produce a usable model altogether~\cite{li2020federated}. The
operational gap is therefore not simply making FL communication faster, but
allowing federation to continue when the network graph itself becomes
fragmented.

Autonomous UAVs acting as data mules offer a way to bridge these disconnected
regions by physically carrying model state between edge devices and aggregation
servers~\cite{zhang2025latency, arsalaan2024uavs}. Doing so, however, introduces
a coordination problem beyond conventional FL. A mule has limited flight time
and energy, so it cannot necessarily visit every device. A useful contact also
depends on whether an update is ready and whether the wireless link can sustain
the transfer when the mule arrives. Existing hierarchical FL, UAV-assisted FL,
physical model transport, RF-adaptive networking, and adaptive client selection
address parts of this problem~\cite{liu2020client, lin2023delay,
parasnis2023connectivity, yemini2023robust, zhang2025latency,
mestoukirdi2022uav, bian2025indirect, wang2018deep, cui2019multi,
nishio2019client, lai2021oort}, but they generally retain persistent
reachability, stationary aggregation, or a fixed communication setting that the
mobility decision does not control. A courier-based federation instead requires
these decisions to work together under a finite mission budget.

In this paper, we present \sysname{}, a Federated RF-aware Routing framework that
sustains federated learning across persistently disconnected regions by flying
UAV data mules between edge devices and an edge server. Its central observation
is that a mule's radio reach is itself a decision. A contact band with a
narrower occupied bandwidth reaches farther at a lower rate: it can serve a
whole field from a single stop at the cost of a longer dwell, whereas a wide
band serves each device quickly but only from nearby, so the mule spends most
of its mission flying between stops. Which trade is better depends on how many
devices need service, where they are, and how much mission time remains, so
\sysname{} chooses the band class and the route together, before each flight,
under the mission budget.

\sysname{} organizes its decisions by when they are made. On the \emph{plan
clock}, at the dock, the mule clusters the devices that need service at each
band class's range, searches routes that pass a single feasibility test (every
stop meets its devices' deadlines, and the mule lands and uploads within the
budget), and commits the plan that serves the most coverage weight, a weight
that grows with the number of missions since a device last contributed. On the
\emph{flight clock}, at each stop, the same test gates a per-stop rule that can
use the realized channel to pick a faster band or reorder the remaining stops,
and the mule re-plans the remainder when the channel has used up the plan's
slack. Updates are merged on the mule with weights that discount stale ones,
and across mules at the server, so rounds close with the updates that arrive
instead of waiting on an unreachable device. Learning can enter in one place, a
learned per-stop score, and the hard gates always run before it. We evaluate
three variants that share the plan: F commits it in flight, FX adds the fixed
per-stop rule, and FQ the learned score.

We implement \sysname{} as a prototype in which the server, each mule and each
device are separate processes that exchange messages over TCP and the devices
train a real intrusion-detection model on CICIoT2023~\cite{CiCIoT2023}, with
mission time, the radio channel and energy simulated. We compare it with seven
whole schedulers, our earlier staged heuristic and six drawn from the
age-of-information, client-selection, UAV-learning and model-transport
literature, on paired seeds and under an analysis plan fixed before the studies
ran. With six devices, one mule and a moderate mission budget, \sysname{}
reaches the target accuracy 27--31\% sooner than each of the seven baselines. The gain comes from shorter rounds, not
fewer: \sysname{}'s plan chooses the long-reach narrow band in 89\% of missions
and cuts the transit between stops from about 140\,s to 15\,s, and pinned to
the wide band it is no faster than FedEx's route. Under tight budgets it keeps
updates fresher than age-of-information and Whittle-index schedulers, and
without its coverage term the share of rounds that close at twelve devices
falls from 99\% to 74\%.
Several design elements show no measurable effect at our settings, and we
report them as such. Among them is learning: FQ performs like F and FX, so the
learned score adds nothing to the fixed rule. In an exploratory comparison,
however, FQ reaches the target 36\% sooner than a learned scheduler that has no
plan, which locates the gain in the plan rather than in learning. We also measure
where \sysname{} falls short: it plans on the mean channel, so it overruns a
tight budget in 30\% of missions, and it does not price training time, so it
becomes less reliable than simpler baselines when devices need time to train.

The contributions of this paper are:

\begin{itemize}

\item \textbf{Reach as a mission decision.} We formulate model transport by
data mules so that the contact band class, which sets how far a mule reaches
and how fast it transfers, is chosen jointly with the route under a mission
budget, and we give a planner that searches both under one feasibility test.

\item \textbf{A two-clock design with bounded learning.} The same feasibility
test gates a dock-time plan and an in-flight per-stop decision, with per-device
deadline windows that adapt to contact outcomes, a coverage weight and age cap
that keep devices from being starved, and staleness-weighted merges on the mule
and at the server. A learned component can rank only the options the gates
admit.

\item \textbf{A prototype and a simulator built from the same code.} The
multi-process prototype trains a real model at every contact, and FerrySim runs
the same planner, flight slot and channel in-process, to train learned
components and to plan for up to 96 devices.

\item \textbf{A pre-registered comparison with the state of the art.} We test
\sysname{} against seven whole schedulers with paired seeds and multiplicity
correction, and report where it wins, why (its band choice), which parts of its
design have no measurable effect, and where it falls short.

\end{itemize}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section~\ref{sec:related_works} reviews related work.
Section~\ref{sec:method} presents \sysname{}'s design: the quantities each
layer supplies, the feasibility test, the two decision clocks, and aggregation.
Section~\ref{sec:setup} describes the experimental setup and the design of
each study, Section~\ref{sec:results} reports and discusses the results
against the state of the art, and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes
and outlines future work.

\section{Related Works}
\label{sec:related_works}

Federated learning reduces centralized data movement by allowing participants to train locally and exchange model updates rather than raw datasets. FedAvg established this model-averaging paradigm, while FedProx improved robustness to statistical and systems heterogeneity \cite{mcmahan2017communication,li2020federated}. Hierarchical approaches subsequently introduced intermediate aggregation to reduce communication cost and accommodate heterogeneous edge environments. Aggregation-oriented hierarchical FL performs partial aggregation at edge servers before cloud synchronization, while delay-aware hierarchical FL explicitly accounts for communication delay between edge and cloud tiers \cite{liu2020client,lin2023delay}. Connectivity-aware semi-decentralized FL further exploits time-varying device-to-device links, and collaborative relaying allows well-connected clients to forward updates for clients experiencing intermittent server connectivity \cite{parasnis2023connectivity,yemini2023robust}. These approaches improve FL under unreliable communication, but they still rely on a communication graph in which model state is eventually forwarded through wireless links. FeRRy targets the more disruptive case in which such an end-to-end path may not exist and model state must instead be physically transported between isolated participants.

UAV-assisted FL introduces mobility into the learning infrastructure, but the role assigned to the UAV varies considerably. A UAV may operate as a mobile FL server whose routing is optimized with bandwidth, computation, and transmit power \cite{zhang2025latency}, or as a mobile orchestrator that visits discrete locations while optimizing routing and device scheduling altogether across multiple FL communities \cite{mestoukirdi2022uav}.  These systems use mobility to restore or improve communication between ground participants and the learning infrastructure. The closest architectural precedent to FeRRy is FedEx, which removes direct client-server connectivity and uses mobile transporters to physically carry model information \cite{bian2025indirect}. FedEx establishes physical model transport and relates FL performance to transporter travel time, but assumes preplanned tours and fixed communication conditions without adapting service to changing RF conditions, per-device deadlines, or in-mission contact opportunities. FeRRy extends this setting by treating reachability, service time, participant urgency, and communication conditions as part of the mission decision itself.

Another research direction studies UAV trajectory planning together with communication-aware data collection. Earlier formulations have demonstrated that trajectory and communication should not be optimized independently, and should jointly optimize multi-UAV trajectories, user scheduling, association, and transmit power for wireless service \cite{wu2018joint}, while more recent learning-based approaches move these decisions online. Multi-UAV controllers have used SNR, reachability, remaining device data, relative distance, and battery state to learn trajectories \cite{chen2023model}, and subsequent work has learned 3-D trajectories and device scheduling \cite{gao2024federated}, incorporated collection deadlines, link quality, and energy constraints through MAPPO \cite{mondal2025deep}, further optimized trajectory and task offloading under AoI, latency, and energy objectives \cite{wang2025joint}, and considered battery and interference constraints in federated-RL data collection \cite{kumar2026battery}. RF adaptation has likewise been studied through deep reinforcement learning for dynamic multichannel access \cite{wang2018deep} and multi-agent resource allocation over users, power levels, and subchannels in UAV networks \cite{cui2019multi}. These studies establish that communication-aware, and energy-aware multi-UAV trajectory learning is already well studied. FeRRy therefore does not claim RF-aware trajectory planning itself as novel, instead, its distinction is that the communication choice directly changes the feasibility and duration of transporting FL updates, while participant urgency determines which contact is worth serving next.

Client-selection and freshness-aware scheduling provides another part of this coordination problem. Existing methods select participants according to round deadlines and resource availability \cite{nishio2019client}, favor clients with higher training loss \cite{cho2022towards}, or use statistical utility and participation history observed in previous rounds \cite{lai2021oort}. This distinction between pre-selection and historical information is particularly important for physical data muling because isolated participants cannot continuously report their current state before the UAV reaches them. Related UAV-FL work has further balanced update age and data value under unstable connectivity \cite{cui2023data}, incorporated freshness into fairness-oriented scheduling \cite{zhu2024fairness}, required devices to be served within a bounded number of slots \cite{zhai2024uav}, and increased the priority of previously failed or unscheduled devices \cite{mestoukirdi2022uav}. These studies establish age-aware ranking and mechanisms to reduce starvation. FeRRy instead focuses on how these concerns interact with physical transport cost, where servicing an old or valuable update also requires flight time, contact time, sufficient radio reach, and remaining mission budget. 

Finally, asynchronous and hierarchical FL research addresses model-version mismatch when participant updates arrive at different times. Prior work has buffered asynchronous client updates before applying server-side aggregation, reducing sensitivity to individual stragglers while remaining compatible with secure aggregation \cite{nguyen2022federated}. Other hierarchical approaches perform asynchronous aggregation across both gateway and cloud tiers while jointly considering device selection and gateway association in heterogeneous IoT environments \cite{yu2023async}. These methods assume that updates are delivered through the network, whereas physical data muling introduces travel time as an additional source of staleness. FeRRy therefore treats aggregation as part of the mission lifecycle, where the same age and deadline information is used to determine whether a participant to be served also influences whether its transported update remains useful when the mule returns. The key distinction is thus the coupling of physical admission, service order, RF-dependent contact feasibility, and update freshness, rather than a new aggregation mechanism in isolation.

Table~\ref{tab:ferry-comparison} shows that prior work addresses individual parts of this problem, including FL-aware participant selection, freshness-aware scheduling, UAV trajectory planning, RF adaptation, and physical model transport. However, even the closest transporter-based approach does not address RF-dependent reach and service time with participant deadlines and in-mission route adaptation. FeRRy addresses this gap by using communication conditions, mobility, and FL-update urgency to plan and revise model transport under a finite mission budget.

\section{\sysname{} Methodology}
\label{sec:method}

\sysname{} sustains federated learning across regions that a stationary network
cannot reach, by flying an autonomous mule (UAV) between edge devices and an
edge server. We describe the design by \emph{decision clock} rather than by
layer, because the two decisions that shape most of its behavior each span the
radio, scheduling and learning layers.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Setting, Layer Roles, and Decision Clocks}
\label{sec:method:roles}

\paragraph{Setting}
A cluster has one edge server, one or more mules, and static field devices whose
positions the server's registry holds. The server gives each mule a disjoint
slice $\mathcal{M}$ of the registry for the trial; with $K>1$ mules the slices
are angular sectors around the dock whose sizes differ by at most one, and the
mules fly concurrently from the shared dock. Devices train offline between
visits, so a contact is exchange only: the mule pushes the current global model
and pulls the device's prepared update. A \emph{mission} has two passes. In
\textsc{Pass 1} the mule collects updates along a route, merges them on board,
and docks to upload; the server merges across mules into the next global model.
In \textsc{Pass 2} the mule delivers that model to every device in its slice,
which gives each later update a known basis version, and so an age. A time
budget $T_{\mathrm{miss}}$ bounds Pass~1: the plan and every check in flight
require the predicted landing and upload to fall within $T_{\mathrm{miss}}$ of
takeoff. Pass~2 is not budgeted.

\paragraph{Learning task}
The devices train a binary intrusion detector on CICIoT2023~\cite{CiCIoT2023},
with 21 features scaled to $[0,1]$. Each trial draws 20{,}000 balanced training
flows, split evenly across the devices, and a disjoint test set of 6{,}000 flows
that is two-thirds benign, so labelling every flow benign scores 0.667. The
model is a multilayer perceptron (hidden layers of 64 to 4 units) trained with
Adam for one local epoch per model received; a device with no prepared update
trains inside the contact, at no simulated cost. The server evaluates each new
global model on the test set, stamped when the closing upload completes. Every
transfer is priced as $S=1$~MB, to represent a larger model than the 18.8~KB
one.

\paragraph{Layer roles}
The radio layer prices a link but never chooses among devices; the scheduling
layer makes every admission, band and route decision; the learning layer values
a collected update and the cost of a missing one (Table~\ref{tab:layer-roles}).
Hard gates (eligibility, the feasibility test, and the age cap) always run
before any ranking, so a ranking rule, learned or not, chooses only among
options the gates admit.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Role of each layer in the joint decisions.}
\label{tab:layer-roles}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{l l L}
\toprule
\textbf{Layer} & \textbf{Role} & \textbf{Supplies to the decisions} \\
\midrule
L1 RF link & prices & Range, rate, dwell, and SNR over time for each band class; backhaul carrier \\
L2 Scheduling & decides & Admission, band class $\bbar$, route, per-arrival (band, next stop), re-plan \\
L3 Federated learning & values & Merge weight, update age, coverage weight, cross-mule merge \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Two decision clocks}
On the \emph{plan clock}, once per mission at the dock, the mule chooses a
contact band class $\bbar$ and an ordered route together, because the band class
fixes the contact range, the range fixes how devices cluster into stops, and
the stops fix the route (Fig.~\ref{fig:clocks}). On the \emph{flight clock}, in
Pass~1, it can revise the band and the next stop from the signal it observes.
The two clocks are needed because interference varies with a period comparable
to one leg, so the band that is best at takeoff need not be best at a later
stop. What the flight observes returns to the plan: rate sets dwell, dwell
advances the mission clock, the clock decides feasibility, and infeasibility
triggers a re-plan. Every decision is a rule or a search over a declared score;
learning can enter only through the flight slot.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Quantities Supplied by the Layers}
\label{sec:method:models}

\subsubsection{L1: Contact Link, Clock, and Backhaul}
\label{sec:method:l1}

\paragraph{Band classes}
The contact link offers a set $\mathcal{B}$ of three band classes that share one
carrier and differ in occupied bandwidth $B_b=N_{\mathrm{RB}}\times180$~kHz, on
LTE channel bandwidths~\cite{3gpp36104}: \textsf{wide} (20~MHz, 100 resource
blocks), \textsf{medium} (5~MHz, 25) and \textsf{narrow} (1.4~MHz, 6). With a
common transmit power and a noise floor that scales with $B_b$, a narrower class
reaches farther at a lower rate. Relative to a reference class with bandwidth
$B_0$ and slant range $R_0^{3D}$,
\begin{equation}
R_b^{3D} = R_0^{3D}\left(\frac{B_0}{B_b}\right)^{1/n},
\qquad
R_b = \sqrt{\left(R_b^{3D}\right)^2 - h^2},
\label{eq:range}
\end{equation}
with path-loss exponent $n=2.2$ and altitude $h=25$~m. Anchoring \textsf{wide} at
60~m gives planar ranges of 60, 120 and 232~m. At $R_b$ the mean SNR exceeds the
decoding floor by a shadowing margin $M_{\mathrm{sh}}=5.1$~dB, so a device at the
edge of its class is reachable with probability 0.9 under shadowing alone.

\paragraph{Rate and dwell}
The mean SNR at distance $d$ is
$\bar\gamma_b(d)=\gamma_{\mathrm{floor}}+M_{\mathrm{sh}}+10\,n\log_{10}(R_b^{3D}/d^{3D})$,
with $\gamma_{\mathrm{floor}}=-6.7$~dB (CQI~1). The rate is the smaller of a CQI
spectral efficiency and the Shannon rate on the occupied bandwidth,
\begin{equation}
r_b(\gamma)=\min\bigl\{\kappa_b B_b\,\mathrm{SE}(\gamma),\;B_b\log_2(1+10^{\gamma/10})\bigr\},
\label{eq:rate}
\end{equation}
for $\gamma\ge\gamma_{\mathrm{floor}}$ and zero below, with $\kappa_b$ an
implementation efficiency. Moving $S_j$ bytes takes
$\tau_{j,b}^{\mathrm{dwell}}(\gamma)=8S_j/r_b(\gamma)$; a Pass-1 session moves
$2S$ (push and pull), a Pass-2 delivery and the upload $S$ each, and the dwells
at one stop add. The channel acts on a contact only through whether a device is
solicited (a device below the floor on arrival is not, and costs no airtime) and
how long its session takes: the rate is read at the session's start, and a
started session always completes. The messages travel over a lossless local TCP
link that carries no radio effects.

\paragraph{Channel over time}
The realized SNR of device $j$ on class $b$ at mission time $t$ is
\begin{equation}
\gamma_{b,j}(t)=\bar\gamma_b(d_j)+X_j(t)+A\sin\bigl(2\pi(t/P_c+\phi_b)\bigr)+\sigma_I\,\xi_b(t),
\label{eq:realsnr}
\end{equation}
with correlated shadowing $X_j$ ($\sigma_{\mathrm{sh}}=4$~dB, correlation time
7.4~s) and a per-class interference term~\cite{3gpp36777} of period $P_c=60$~s,
class phases $\phi_b\in\{0,\tfrac13,\tfrac23\}$ and noise $\xi_b$; in the
interference-limited (``jittery'') regime used throughout, $A=5$~dB and
$\sigma_I=1.5$~dB. Both terms come from keyed hashes, so two policies that ask for
the same value at the same time get the same value. The planner prices only the
mean $\bar\gamma_b$, since pricing the realized phase would be an oracle, so
realized missions run longer than planned; the flight clock observes
$\gamma_{b,j}(t)$. The planner also uses the outage probability
\begin{equation}
p_{\mathrm{out}}(b,d)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{floor}}-\bar\gamma_b(d)}{\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right),
\quad
\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}^2=\sigma_{\mathrm{sh}}^2+\sigma_I^2+\tfrac{A^2}{2}.
\label{eq:pout}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Mission clock and energy}
Mission time is a simulated clock charged for transit at 5~m/s, dwell, a 1~s
listen window at a stop with a missing reply, the return leg, the upload, and a
30~s dock turnaround. Energy follows the same ledger,
\begin{equation}
E = P_{\mathrm{move}}\,(t_{\mathrm{transit}}+t_{\mathrm{return}})
  + P_{\mathrm{hover}}\,(t_{\mathrm{dwell}}+t_{\mathrm{listen}}),
\label{eq:energy}
\end{equation}
with $P_{\mathrm{move}}=143.6$~W and $P_{\mathrm{hover}}=168.5$~W from the
rotary-wing model of Zeng et al.~\cite{zeng2019energy}. Flight is planar at
altitude $h$, energy counts propulsion only, and no battery capacity is enforced.

\paragraph{Backhaul}
The upload rides the best of three backhaul carriers and is lost with a fixed
probability (2\%). A lost upload is not retried: the server returns the
unchanged model, Pass~2 delivers it, and the planner, which records the devices
as merged before the upload, still counts them as served. The component
ablations' backhaul test and every cell of the radio study
(Table~\ref{tab:studies}) use a time-varying backhaul instead, whose SNR
swings sinusoidally and whose loss is logistic in the SNR; on the fixed carrier
it loses about a fifth of the uploads (F closes 79\% of its rounds there,
against 97\%). Only there does the radio layer's adaptive carrier controller
(F+L1) act, and since it observes the realized SNR that decides each loss, it is
close to an oracle. The backhaul never enters a scheduling decision.

\subsubsection{L2/L3: Demand, Deadlines, Ages, and the Age Cap}
\label{sec:method:demand}

\paragraph{Contact outcomes}
A Pass-1 contact is \emph{clean} when the device returns an update matching the
round, size and checksum the mule expects, \emph{partial} when the device
answers but refuses or fails those checks, and otherwise a \emph{timeout}.
Whether a reachable device replies is drawn each mission from its reliability
$\rho_j\sim U(0.15,1)$; a device whose reply is lost still receives the push and
adopts the model. A wall-clock session timeout (36~s at $N=6$) is recorded as a
timeout; at 0.75, 1 and 1.5 times its value the results were identical. To study
compute heterogeneity, a device can take a log-normal time to train, restarted
by each model it receives; an update not ready on arrival is a timeout that costs
no airtime. The plan does not price training time.

\paragraph{Per-device deadline}
Each device $j$ carries a fulfilment window $\Phi(j)$ and a deadline
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Deadline}(j)=t+\Phi(j)-\iota(j),
\label{eq:deadline}
\end{equation}
where $t$ is the planning time and $\iota(j)$ the time since its last clean
contact. After each contact the window is scaled and clamped,
\begin{equation}
\Phi(j)\leftarrow\min\{\Phi_{\max},\max\{\Phi_{\min},\,\beta_{o}\,\Phi(j)\}\},
\label{eq:phi}
\end{equation}
with $\beta_{\mathrm{clean}}=0.8$; $\beta_{\mathrm{partial}}=1.25$ for a partial
or a timeout after the device answered (a failed push, a lost reply, or no
update ready); and $\beta_{\mathrm{timeout}}=1.5$ for a device that stayed
silent, was out of reach, or was left out. Windows are in units of
$\sigma=\Tnom/10$~s, where $\Tnom$ is the median duration of a nominal two-pass
mission on the wide band (203~s at $N=6$): $\Phi_0=60\sigma$, $\Phi_{\min}=5\sigma$
and $\Phi_{\max}=300\sigma$~s. A clean contact re-anchors $\iota(j)$; a failed one
widens the window but leaves the anchor stale, so a device that keeps failing
grows steadily more overdue. A device the plan leaves out, or the mule drops in
flight, is recorded as a synthetic timeout.

\paragraph{Ages and coverage weight}
The \emph{plan age} $a_j=m-U_j$ counts the missions of the device's own mule
since the mission $U_j$ whose merge last used its update; a high plan age
strengthens the device's claim to be served. The \emph{merge age} $a_i=v-b_i$
of an update is the version $v$ of the model the mule carries minus the version
$b_i$ the device trained from, which the device echoes with its update; it
discounts the update in the merge. A missed contact relaxes a device's
\emph{window} but not its \emph{priority}, which enters through the coverage
weight
\begin{equation}
w_j=\max(a_j,1)\,(1+\mu_j),
\label{eq:covweight}
\end{equation}
where $\mu_j$ is the miss streak; under a plan, $\mu_j=a_j-1$, so $w_j$ grows
roughly as $a_j^2$.

\paragraph{Age cap}
A device is \emph{capped} when $a_j\ge S$. A pilot sets $S=2$, the fewest
missions that serve every servable device on 90\% of sampled layouts at the
stress budget. A stop's own deadline is the earliest among its uncapped members,
and a stop of capped members only is exempt from its deadline clause but not
from the budget. A trimmed route flies stops with a capped member first; a
capped device its stop cannot serve within the budget gets a one-device
\emph{hover stop} between it and the dock; and the plan key first compares the
ages of the capped devices a plan leaves out.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{The Feasibility Test and the Mission Clock}
\label{sec:method:gate}

One predicate decides whether a stop may be served next; it is the only
admission rule in the plan-mode system, applied to the committed plan, inside
the plan search, at every departure, inside the re-plan, and to the in-flight
choices. For a stop $s$ with members $\mathcal{M}_s$, reached from a state
(pose, clock $c$, energy) on band $b$,
\begin{align}
t_{\mathrm{arr}} &= c+\|\mathrm{pose}-s\|/v,\\
t_{\mathrm{fin}} &= t_{\mathrm{arr}}+\!\!\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}_s}\!\tau^{\mathrm{dwell}}_{j,b}(\bar\gamma_b(d_j)),\\
t_{\mathrm{home}} &= t_{\mathrm{fin}}+t_{\mathrm{return}}+t_{\mathrm{upload}},
\end{align}
and the stop is admitted only if (i) $t_{\mathrm{fin}}$ meets the stop's own
deadline, (ii) $t_{\mathrm{home}}$ falls within the budget, takeoff plus
$T_{\mathrm{miss}}$, and (iii) the energy of Eq.~\eqref{eq:energy} stays within
capacity, if one is set. Every clause is monotone in the member set, so a stop
that fails whole can be reduced to the members that fit. The test prices the
mean SNR, so the realized channel can lengthen an admitted stop; the departure
check catches this after the stop, but nothing re-checks after the last Pass-1
stop, so a realized mission can overrun the budget.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Plan Clock: Reach and Route}
\label{sec:method:plan}

At the dock the mule commits a plan $\mathcal{P}=(\bbar,\pi)$: the band class
flown in both passes, and an ordered list of stops, each reduced to the members
that fit. The demand is every device in the slice, with its deadline, plan age,
miss streak and weight.

\paragraph{Reach is a decision}
For each class $b$, a greedy anchor sweep clusters the demand into stops at the
class's range $R_b$, at a cluster's centroid when every member is within $R_b$
of it. A wide class serves few devices per stop at a high rate; a narrow class
can reach the field from one stop but dwells longer. No fixed rule chooses
between them, so the planner prices every class and commits the best.

\paragraph{Route search}
Candidate routes pass through the feasibility test stop by stop. Up to six
demanded devices, an \textsf{exact} search enumerates every ordered sequence of
stops and member subsets, pruning failing prefixes, and is optimal over what the
score prices. With more devices but at most six stops, it searches ordered stop
subsets, trimming each stop greedily; beyond that, a bounded local search
(2-OPT, then first-improvement moves, at most 2000 evaluations per class) keeps
planning deterministic. The empty plan is chosen only if no other is admitted.

\paragraph{Plan score and plan key}
Candidates are scored by
\begin{equation}
V(\bbar,\pi)=-\Bigl[c_1\Bigl(\tfrac{\Delta}{\Tnom}\Bigr)^{2}+c_2U+c_3L+c_4\frac{E}{P_{\mathrm{hover}}\Tnom}\Bigr],
\label{eq:planscore}
\end{equation}
where $\Delta$ is the duration of the whole two-pass mission on $\bbar$, $E$ its
energy, and
\begin{equation}
U=1-\frac{\sum_{\text{served}}w_j}{\sum_{\text{demand}}w_j},
\qquad
L=\frac{\sum_{\text{served}}w_j\,p_{\mathrm{out}}(\bbar,d_j)}{\sum_{\text{demand}}w_j}
\end{equation}
the weighted coverage shortfall and expected link loss, with $c_1=1$,
$c_2=c_3=N_{\mathrm{demand}}$ and $c_4=0.1$. The form follows FedEx's
route-dependent bound~\cite{bian2025indirect}, but the score is declared, not
derived: the constants are hand-set and the term in $\Delta$ is a staleness
surrogate. Because every plan that serves a device pays for a whole Pass~2, $V$
alone can prefer to fly empty, so the mule commits the plan with the smallest
key
\begin{equation}
\bigl(\kappa_{\mathrm{cap}},\;-\textstyle\sum_{\text{served}}w_j/\sum_{\text{demand}}w_j,\;-V,\;\text{class index}\bigr),
\label{eq:plankey}
\end{equation}
compared lexicographically, where $\kappa_{\mathrm{cap}}$ lists the ages of the
capped devices the plan leaves out, largest first. Time and energy thus break
ties among plans that serve the same weight, and the order of enumeration never
matters. A guard fold re-checks the chosen route before commit, and every
device the plan leaves out is recorded as a miss. No plan-time value is learned.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Flight Clock: Band, Next Stop, and Re-Planning}
\label{sec:method:flight}

\paragraph{The flight slot}
In Pass~1, after takeoff, the mule can revise two choices per stop: the band on
which to serve the stop it has reached, and the next stop of the remaining
queue. With an empty slot, \sysname{} flies the plan's band and order unchanged;
this is F, the reference arm. The fixed filling, FX, is a cross-layer rule that
makes the two choices at different moments: on arrival it picks the fastest
class that still reaches every device $\bbar$ reaches at the stop, at the
observed SNR; at the next departure, after the stop is served and the departure
check has run, it picks the nearest remaining stop whose move to the front still
passes the feasibility test from the realized clock, or else the plan's next.

The learned filling, FQ, makes both choices on arrival, as a pair $(b,s)$ ranked
by a learned score. A pair is admitted only if the band reaches every device
$\bbar$ reaches at the stop, the next stop belongs to the plan, and the rest of
the flight still passes the feasibility test after serving on $b$ at the
observed dwell; if no pair is admitted, the mule serves on FX's band and keeps
the plan's order. The score is a masked double DQN over one feature row per
admitted pair (the current and next-stop SNR per class, the dwell, deadline
slack, plan ages, the clock and energy left, and the phase of the interference
cycle), trained in FerrySim on a per-stop reward: the merge weight collected less
a time cost, with the weighted shortfall of committed devices charged at the end
of each sortie. FQ thus picks its next stop before serving, from the priced
dwell, and FX after serving, from the realized clock.

\paragraph{Departure check and re-plan}
After each stop, the mule checks the remaining queue against the feasibility
test at its current clock. If the queue no longer fits, it re-plans the
remainder: stops with a capped member move to the front, the rest keep the
plan's order, and stops and members that no longer fit are trimmed. Every
dropped stop is final for the mission and recorded as a synthetic timeout.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Aggregation: Mule, Cluster, and Delivery}
\label{sec:method:merge}

\paragraph{Merge on the mule}
Devices send the update $\Delta\theta_i=\theta_i^{\mathrm{after}}-\theta_i^{\mathrm{basis}}$
with its basis version. At the end of Pass~1 the mule merges the updates with
age-dependent weights,
\begin{equation}
w_i=n_i\,v_i\,s(a_i)\ \text{ for } a_i\le a_{\max,j},\qquad w_i=0\ \text{ otherwise},
\label{eq:mergeweight}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
M=\sum_{i\,\text{admitted}}n_iv_i,\qquad
\Delta_m=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i\,\text{admitted}}w_i\,\Delta\theta_i,
\label{eq:mulemerge}
\end{equation}
where $n_i$ is the number of local examples and $v_i$ a value proxy (uniform in
the evaluation). The staleness factor is FedAsync's hinge~\cite{xie2019asynchronous},
$s(a)=1/(a+1)$, and the cutoff comes from the device's own window,
$a_{\max,j}=\lfloor\Phi(j)/\Tnom\rfloor$, so the window that admits a device
(Eq.~\eqref{eq:deadline}) also bounds how long its update counts. Dividing by
$M$ rather than $\sum w_i$ lets a uniformly stale mission move the model by
only $s(a)$ times its mean; with current bases the merge is the plain
example-weighted mean, as it is for almost every merge on the mule in our runs.

\paragraph{Merge across mules}
At the server, each mule's partial carries its own staleness $s_m=s(V-v_m)$,
where $V$ is the server's version and $v_m$ the version the mule carried:
\begin{equation}
\theta\leftarrow\theta+\eta\,\frac{\sum_{m\,\text{live}}M_m\,s_m\,\Delta_m}{\sum_{m\,\text{live}}M_m},
\label{eq:clustermerge}
\end{equation}
with $\eta=1$; a partial is live if non-empty. The server merges as soon as one
partial arrives, so each upload closes its own round and no round waits on an
unreachable device. A mule flies Pass~1 with the model it received at its
previous dock, so with several mules the others' merges in between make its
partial stale: at $N=6$ with three mules, 160 of 198 merges applied a partial one
to three versions old, discounted to between a half and a quarter of its weight.

\paragraph{Delivery}
If Pass~1 collected any update, the mule flies Pass~2: it delivers the new model
to every stop of its slice at $R(\bbar)$, nearest first, on $\bbar$, skipping only
a device below the floor on arrival. Each device stores the model with its
version and resumes offline training.

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Mission Round, Cost, and Implementation}
\label{sec:method:alg}

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{One \sysname{} mission round}
\label{alg:mission}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require Slice $\mathcal{M}$, model $\theta$ with version $v$, budget $T_{\mathrm{miss}}$, cap $S$
\Statex \textbf{[Dock: plan clock]}
\State Take slice $\mathcal{M}$ and the model $\theta$ (version $v$) received at the previous dock; compute demand, weights $w_j$, capped set
\For{each band class $b\in\mathcal{B}$}
  \State $\textit{stops}_b\gets$ cluster demand at $R_b$ and add hover stops for capped devices
  \State $\mathcal{P}_b\gets$ \textsc{Search}$(\textit{stops}_b)$ under the feasibility test
\EndFor
\State $(\bbar,\pi)\gets$ plan with the smallest key (Eq.~\ref{eq:plankey}); guard fold; commit; record left-out devices as misses
\Statex \textbf{[Pass 1: flight clock]}
\For{each stop $s_k$ in the queue}
  \State Fly to $s_k$; observe $\gamma_{b,j}(t)$ for all classes
  \State Band $b_k$: $\bbar$ (F); fastest covering class (FX); with $s_{k+1}$, best admitted pair (FQ)
  \State Serve members on $b_k$; update $\Phi(j)$ and $\iota(j)$ from each outcome
  \If{remainder does not pass the feasibility test}
    \State Re-plan by trimming; record dropped stops as timeouts
  \EndIf
  \State Next stop: plan order (F); nearest that keeps the remainder feasible (FX); the pair's (FQ)
\EndFor
\State Merge on the mule with cutoff (Eq.~\ref{eq:mulemerge}); fly to the dock; upload
\Statex \textbf{[Dock: server]}
\State Server merges across mules (Eq.~\ref{eq:clustermerge}) to obtain $\theta'$ with version $v+1$
\Statex \textbf{[Pass 2, if Pass 1 collected any update]}
\For{each stop in nearest-first order from the dock}
  \State Deliver $\theta'$ on $\bbar$; devices resume offline training
\EndFor
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Cost}
Training stays on the devices. The \textsf{exact} search evaluates at most 1957
stop sequences per class, and the local search at most 2000, so planning cost
does not depend on wall time; each arrival evaluates at most
$|\mathcal{B}|\times|\text{queue}|$ pairs, one feasibility fold each, and both
merges are linear in their inputs.

\paragraph{Implementation, scope, and FerrySim}
The prototype runs the server, each mule and each device as separate Python
processes that exchange messages over TCP, and the devices train the real model;
mission time, the radio channel and energy are simulated, not measured. Updates
carry integrity checks but no authentication; poisoning-robust aggregation and
privacy mechanisms are out of scope. The learned score, the learned baseline E3,
and the largest problems ($N=48$ and $96$) run in FerrySim, an in-process
simulator built from the same driver, services, planner, flight slot,
feasibility test, channel and clock. It omits model training (a device returns
the global model plus small noise), flies one mule, uses an additive deadline
law and no merge cutoff, and grows the field with $N$ in its scale cells, so its
$N=24$ is not the full system's.

\section{Experimental Setup and Design}
\label{sec:setup}

\subsection{Testbed}
\label{sec:setup:testbed}

Every trial runs the full system described above: the server, each
mule, and each device are separate processes that exchange messages over TCP,
and the devices train the real intrusion-detection model on CICIoT2023.
Mission time, the radio channel, and energy come from the simulated clock and
channel described above, in the interference-limited (jittery)
regime. A trial flies four missions with a 1~MB model payload and records every
event, from which a separate scorer computes the metrics. The learned per-stop
score and the learned baseline E3 are trained in FerrySim, which also runs the
largest problems ($N=48$ and $96$).

\subsection{Cells, Budgets, and the Accuracy Target}
\label{sec:setup:cells}

A cell fixes the number of devices $N$, the number of mules $K$, and the mission
budget. Devices are static and placed uniformly at random on a $200\times200$~m
square centred on the dock, a new layout per trial; the square is the same at
every $N$, so the field grows denser as $N$ grows (FerrySim's scale cells grow
it instead). We evaluate $N\in\{6,12,24\}$ devices with one mule, and up to three
mules at $N=12$ and $18$. Each $N$ has two mission budgets, set by pilots before
the studies ran. The \emph{knee} is the smallest budget whose mean update yield
reaches 95\% of the best on a budget grid (150, 180 and 262\,s at $N=6$, 12 and
24), and the \emph{stress} budget is half of it. The accuracy target
$\tau=0.71$ is the largest value, on a 0.01 grid, that at least 80\% of the
baseline H1's trials reach at every $N$'s knee. It lies 4.3 points above the
0.667 that labelling every test flow benign would score, so time to $\tau$ measures how soon a model
becomes useful, not how good it ends; Table~\ref{tab:exp5_headline} also reports
F's and H0's final accuracy. The age cap is $S=2$.

\subsection{Arms}
\label{sec:setup:arms}

Table~\ref{tab:exp5_arms} lists the arms. \sysname{} has three, which share the
dock-time plan and differ only in how they fill the flight slot: F leaves it empty and flies the plan as
committed, FX fills it with the fixed cross-layer rule, and FQ with the learned
pair score. Every baseline is a whole scheduler,
flown in the same simulator, at the same budgets, on the same seeds, and on the
wide contact band. Each baseline's departure from its paper is stated in the
table: for instance, D3 flies our expected-connectivity variant of Cui et al.'s
index, D4 runs FedEx's tour with one transporter, and D5 is FedCS without its
resource-request phase.

plan and differ only in the in-flight slot; the baselines are whole schedulers flown on
the same simulator, budgets and paired seeds.}
\label{tab:exp5_arms}
\small

\paragraph{How the baselines fly}
The baselines share \sysname{}'s first stages: they cluster the devices into
stops at the wide band's range, price a stop with the same feasibility test,
and deliver in an unbudgeted, nearest-first Pass~2. Unlike \sysname{}, they
serve whole stops only, have no age cap, and use an additive deadline law: a
device's window shrinks by $5\sigma$~s after a clean contact and widens by
$10\sigma$~s after a miss, with a floor of $5\sigma$~s and no ceiling. H1 admits
stops in deadline order under the deadline and budget clauses, flies them by
priority bucket (new devices first) and then by distance from the dock, and
trims at each departure as \sysname{} does. D1--D3 rank the stops by their own
key (age of information, statistical utility, the Whittle index) and walk the
ranking under the budget clause alone, skipping what fails; D5 adds stops in
order of least marginal time while they fit one round deadline. These four fly
their admitted order, re-check only the budget at each departure, and re-admit
by their own rule. D4 flies FedEx's visit-all tour with no budget check, so it
can overrun the budget, and with three mules it splits the devices by FedEx's
own assignment rather than by sectors. E3 admits every stop and, at takeoff and
at each departure, picks the next stop by its learned Q-values among the stops
that still fit the budget, with no re-plan. It is trained in FerrySim with one
mule (learning rate $5\times10^{-4}$, $\gamma=0.99$) and flown per mule with
three.

\subsection{Metrics and Statistics}
\label{sec:setup:metrics}

The primary metric is the simulated time to $\tau$: from the first takeoff to
the first evaluation of the global model that reaches $\tau$. We also report the
network age of updates (the mean number of missions since each device's last
merged update), the round-close rate, the deadline-miss rate, the update yield
(updates merged per round), and the mission energy. Trials are paired by seed,
so every arm in a cell sees the same layout, channel and data. Each comparison
is the paired mean difference with a 95\% percentile-bootstrap CI (2000
resamples) and a Wilcoxon signed-rank $p$, Holm-corrected across each study's
comparisons. A comparison is a \emph{claim} when the CI excludes 0 and the Holm
$p<0.05$. Each study's cells, arms, primary metric and reference arm, the test
families, and the pilot rules were fixed in an analysis plan before the studies
ran.

\subsection{Experiment Design}
\label{sec:setup:design}

The evaluation answers six questions: Q1, does \sysname{} beat the state of the
art; Q2, where does its advantage come from; Q3, how does it scale, and what does
deciding cost; Q4, does each part of its design matter; Q5, does learning help
inside its plan; and Q6, how robust is it. Table~\ref{tab:studies} lists the
studies that answer them. Each study's cells, arms, primary metric and Holm
family were fixed in our analysis plan before the studies ran;
unless stated, a study flies one mule with 20 paired trials per cell. Q4 tests
five claims about the design, each against an alternative that removes or
replaces one part of it: C1, reach is a decision; C2, one derived objective; C3,
one deadline in three roles; C4, two clocks, re-decided per stop; and C5,
fairness under physical cost. For Q2, the scheduler comparison's traces also
split each arm's mission time into transit, dwell, and the return, upload and
turnaround. The learned-score study trains the learned pair score at six
discount factors, ten seeds each, and keeps it only if some $\gamma$ beats
$\gamma=0$ by $\epsilon=0.01$ in held-out return over 1000 episodes per cell.
The FQ-vs-E3 comparison was added after that verdict, so it is exploratory and
Holm-corrected across its own eight comparisons; H0, which has no mule, is
described rather than tested.

\paragraph{What was run}
To meet the submission date, we cut the later studies. The merge-rule,
deadline-form and objective-terms studies, the learned score's full-system
check, and the scheduler comparison's two added baselines (D5 and E3) flew 20 of
their planned 40 trials per cell. We dropped the merge-rule study's H1 route with
an unbudgeted Pass~2, the scheduler comparison's relaxed budget, the band-pinning
study's range-ratio and far-device settings, the fairness study's eight-mission
horizon, the scale study's two- and three-mule cells and its clean channel, the
training-time study's measured and 10~MB payloads, the non-IID study's Dirichlet
$\alpha=1$ and quantity-skew partitions, and the radio study's adaptive-backhaul
arms. Two planned studies did not run: one on when learning helps, and one on
real radios, which awaits testbed access. The remaining trials extend the same seeds. FQ was planned in the
scheduler comparison and the scale study but left them, as the plan specified,
when the learned-score study did not keep the learned score; its later flights
are the exploratory FQ-vs-E3 comparison.

\section{Evaluation Results and Discussion}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Against the State of the Art}
\label{sec:res:sota}

Table~\ref{tab:exp5_headline} sets FeRRy against every baseline at $N=6$. With
one mule at the knee budget, F reaches $\tau$ in 194\,s, and each of the seven
baselines needs 264--282\,s: F is 27--31\% faster, and every comparison is a
claim. FedEx with its own merge (D4$_{\text{FedEx}}$), a variant of D4, is as
slow (281\,s) but misses $\tau$ in one trial, and its comparison is not a claim. Paired seed by seed, F reaches $\tau$ first in 80--90\% of the trials
against each baseline. FeRRy's other two arms are as fast: FX reaches $\tau$ in
178\,s and FQ in 180\,s, and neither differs significantly from F. FQ, flown
after the pre-registered study, is also faster than D4 and E3 at the knee in
its own exploratory family (Holm $p<0.001$). Under the stress budget, only the FedEx route (D4) is
significantly slower. The other baselines trail by 28--60\,s, but they keep
within the budget by leaving devices out, which widens their spread. With three
mules every scheduler reaches $\tau$ in 52--65\,s, except FedEx with its own
merge (D4$_{\text{FedEx}}$), which needs 101\,s: its unweighted accumulation of
one-tour-old updates slows learning. Without a mule (H0), federated learning
over the degraded live link merges 0.5 updates per round and ends at an
accuracy of 0.686, barely above the 0.667 of labelling every flow benign,
against F's 3.5 updates and 0.831.

\subsection{Why FeRRy Is Faster: Reach}
\label{sec:res:mechanism}

F does not need fewer rounds than the baselines: all of them reach $\tau$ in
1.65--1.84 rounds on average, with near-identical update yield. F's rounds are
shorter. Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_mechanism} shows where a mission's time goes. Every
baseline flies the wide band, which reaches a device only from nearby, so it
spends about 140\,s of a mission in transit between stops. F's plan chooses the
narrow band in 89\% of missions: its range covers the field from about one
stop, so F spends 15\,s in transit and 107\,s dwelling at the lower rate, and
its missions are 22--26\% shorter. FX and FQ inherit the plan's reach: they fly the
narrow or medium band on 95\% and 98\% of missions and spend the same 15\,s in
transit (Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_learning}b). Pinning F to each band class isolates this
effect: pinned to the wide band, F reaches $\tau$ in 265\,s, D4's own time;
pinned to the narrow band, in 196\,s, F's own. (The band-pinning study's pre-registered
metric is the age of updates, on which the pinned bands do not differ; these
times to $\tau$ are descriptive.) The choice also adapts
(Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_bands}). As the field fills and the budget tightens, F
shifts to the faster medium and wide classes, mostly wide at $N=24$ under the
stress budget, where the narrow band's dwell would no longer fit.

\subsection{Scale and Decision Cost}
\label{sec:res:scale}

Table~\ref{tab:exp5_scale} follows the comparison to larger fields. At $N=24$, F
is significantly faster than H1 and D3 at the knee (749 against 951 and 911\,s)
and ties the FedEx route (752\,s); under the stress budget it beats the FedEx
route (661 against 752\,s). At $N=12$ no comparison is a claim; FQ, flown in the
same cells in the learned-score study's full-system check, takes 461\,s at the knee and 389\,s under
the stress budget, not significantly different from FX (424 and 386\,s). FeRRy's planning
stays affordable (Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_systems}a): the planner takes 0.04\,s per
plan at $N=6$ and 1.5\,s at $N=96$ (p95 2.0\,s), a small share of a mission.
In FerrySim, the plan serves 54--57\% of the devices at each scale's knee
budget from $N=24$ to $96$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_systems}b). Adding mules divides
the work: at $N=12$, F's time to $\tau$ falls from 486\,s with one mule to
226\,s with two and 151\,s with three (Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_systems}c).

\subsection{The Design Claims}
\label{sec:res:claims}

Table~\ref{tab:exp5_claims} tests each claim against an alternative that
removes or replaces one part of FeRRy's design. Five tests hold. The coverage
term keeps rounds closing: without it, the round-close rate falls from 99\% to
74\% (C2). FeRRy keeps updates fresher than the fairness baselines under the
stress budget: its network age of updates is 0.78 missions, against 1.06 for
MAX-AoI and 1.07 for Cui's Whittle index, and 1.10 without the coverage term
(C5). On the time-varying backhaul, the adaptive controller lowers it from
0.88 to 0.69. That controller observes the SNR that decides each upload's loss, so this is close to the most that adapting the
backhaul can give. Several parts of the
design show no measurable effect at these settings, and we report them as such.
Pinning the band does not change the age of updates (its effect is on time). The dwell term and the age cap change nothing
over four missions. The merge rules tie: with every device served in Pass~2,
collected updates almost always have merge age zero, so the age weighting
rarely acts; FedBuff's buffering slows learning, and FedProx is not
significantly faster. The selection literature's deadline forms miss slightly
more deadlines than FeRRy's per-device deadline (47\% against 42\% under the
stress budget), but not significantly.

\subsection{Learning Inside the Plan}
\label{sec:res:rl}

The learned-score study's result is flat: no $\gamma$ beats $\gamma=0$ by the pre-registered
margin, and the best learned score ($\gamma=0.75$) matches FeRRy's fixed rule
(FX) while trailing the one-step greedy rule. In the full system FQ is again
indistinguishable from FX at $N=12$ (C4 in Table~\ref{tab:exp5_claims}), as it is
from F and FX at $N=6$ (Table~\ref{tab:exp5_headline}). FX is therefore FeRRy's
per-stop rule, and the null is reported here. The two do not decide on the
same information: FQ picks its next stop on arrival, from the priced dwell, and
FX after serving, from the realized clock, so
the comparison is of two rules, not of two rankings over the same choice.

\paragraph{Learning inside the plan, against learning without one}
The exploratory comparison asks how a learner inside FeRRy's plan fares against
a published learned scheduler. FQ, FeRRy's plan with the $\gamma=0.75$ score,
flew the scheduler comparison's one-mule cells on the same 20 seeds as E3, our single-agent DQN after
Chen et al.~\cite{chen2023model}, which picks every next stop with no dock-time
plan (Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_learning}). At the knee budget FQ reaches $\tau$ in 180\,s
against E3's 280\,s, a paired difference of 100\,s (95\% CI [63, 141]; Holm
$p<0.001$ across the eight exploratory comparisons). Under the stress budget, FQ
is faster over the 19 seeds in which both reach $\tau$ (174 against 211\,s), but
the CI includes zero. FQ is indistinguishable from F and FX at both budgets. Its
advantage therefore comes from the plan, not from learning. FQ inherits the
plan's choice of band (narrow or medium on 98\% of missions) and spends 15\,s of
a 155\,s mission in transit, whereas E3 flies the wide band and spends 144\,s of
a 228\,s mission in transit. The same ordering holds in FerrySim, where each
learner is scored on its own objective: E3's held-out return falls 6\% below
FX's, while FQ's matches FX's. We did not build a single learner that also makes
the plan's decisions, so this is our closest test of a learner inside FeRRy's
plan and gates against one without them. It supports the two-clock structure
(C4), not a gain from learning.

\subsection{Robustness and Limitations}
\label{sec:res:robust}

Table~\ref{tab:exp5_robust} varies the data, the channel and the devices'
compute. With strongly non-IID data (Dirichlet $\alpha=0.1$), every arm reaches
$\tau$ in only about half of the trials, and F remains significantly faster than
H1 and D3 where both reach it. The radio study flies the time-varying backhaul
throughout, so its default column (F at 216\,s) is not the main configuration
(194\,s). Under its harsher channels F stays ahead of H1 without a claim, and
FX's per-stop rule is significantly faster than F on the default channel and
with 8\,dB shadowing. Two limitations stand out.
First, FeRRy's plan prices the mean SNR, so under the stress budget 30\% of its
missions overrun the budget, by 8.5\,s on average
(Fig.~\ref{fig:exp5_budget}); the FedEx route, which never skips a device,
overruns in 85\%. Second, when devices take time to train (the training-time study), F's
update yield falls from 3.5 to 0.7 updates per round and it reaches $\tau$ in
only 70--75\% of trials, while H1, D4 and D5 keep 85--100\%: FeRRy's plan does
not price training time, so it reaches devices whose updates are not ready.
Adding a compute term to the plan is future work.

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This paper presented \sysname{}, a framework that sustains federated learning
across disconnected regions by planning UAV data-mule missions in which the
radio's reach is a decision. At the dock, \sysname{} chooses a contact band
class and a route together under one feasibility test that respects per-device
deadlines and the mission budget. In flight, the same test gates a per-stop
decision and a re-plan, and staleness-weighted merges on the mule and at the
server close rounds with the updates that arrive. In a multi-process prototype
that trains a real intrusion-detection model, \sysname{} reached the target
accuracy 27--31\% sooner than seven whole schedulers at six devices, because its
plan chose a long-reach narrow band that removed most of the transit between
stops. It kept updates fresher than age-of-information schedulers under tight
budgets, beat the FedEx route at 24 devices under the stress budget, and planned
in 1.5\,s at 96 devices. Several elements of the design showed no measurable
effect at our settings. Among them is a learned per-stop score: FQ performed like
the fixed rule, and its exploratory advantage over a learned scheduler without a
plan came from the plan it flies inside.

Future work follows from the limitations we measured. \sysname{}'s plan prices
the mean channel, so it overran tight budgets in 30\% of missions; pricing the
channel's variation, or reserving slack for it, is a first step. The plan also
ignores training time, so when devices need time to train it reaches devices
whose updates are not ready; adding a compute term to the plan is a second.
Beyond these, mission time, the radio channel and energy are simulated in this
evaluation. Validating the band trade over the air on a UAV testbed, with
measured channels and battery limits, and coordinating mules that share
spectrum and a dock remain open.
